# Week 12: Consolidation {.unnumbered}

::: {.week-meta}
Core reading
: None: this week is for consolidation

Data
: [Student Life Survey](../course/dataset.qmd) or your own data

App
: None

Task style
: Application: apply the technique to the Student Life Survey (or your own data) with a checklist

## By the end of this week you can

- Explain and defend your measurement and structural models from start to finish.
- Identify what is still unclear from Weeks 0–11.
- Begin your results draft.

## Warm-up

Answer from memory at the start of the session. It takes two minutes and makes earlier ideas easier to recall later.

1. What is the two-step approach?
2. Why does a regression model have 0 df?
3. Which Amos options are unavailable when the data have missing values? (Week 9)

<details class="answers">
<summary>Check your answers</summary>

1. Test the measurement model first, then add the structural model.
2. It estimates as many parameters as there are variances and covariances.
3. Modification indices, tests for normality and outliers, and the bootstrap.

</details>

## This week in brief

No new material. You present your analysis so far, we work through the "still unclear" items in your log, and you start writing. From now on the SEM log has a second part: a running draft of your results section, which becomes the capstone.

## Before the session

Reread your SEM log. Prepare a 10-minute walk-through of your screening, measurement model and structural model.

## In the session

- Your walk-through, with questions.
- The unclear items from your log.
- The structure of a results section, using the [capstone rubric](week-17.qmd#capstone-rubric).

## Your task this week

Start your results draft with two subsections, using the rubric:

1. **Data screening and missing data** (from Weeks 8 and 9).
2. **Measurement model** (from Weeks 3–7): fit, loadings, reliability and validity, and every change with its justification.

## For your SEM log

Write your answers in your log first; then compare.

1. Which decision so far was hardest to justify, and how did you justify it?
2. What would you do differently if you started the analysis again?

<details class="answers model">
<summary>Compare with model answers (after writing your own)</summary>

1. There is no single answer. A strong answer names the decision (for example, freeing an error covariance), the evidence (MI, wording), the alternative and why it was rejected.
2. A strong answer usually mentions planning: deciding the model and the criteria for changes before looking at modification indices.

</details>

## Checkpoint

You have now finished the single-group weeks.

- [ ] I can screen data and justify how I handled problems and missing values.
- [ ] I can fit and defend a measurement model.
- [ ] I can fit a structural model and report direct and indirect effects.
- [ ] I have written the first two subsections of my results draft.

Anything you cannot yet tick is the first item for the next session.
